claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been synthesized in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A hybrid physics-informed machine-learning workflow can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed workflow will be more accurate and computationally efficient than high-throughput ab initio and CALPHAD methods.
Chemical-clustering metrics, local misfit volumes, and phase-distribution statistics can serve as reduced-order descriptors of the hierarchical heterostructure.
Chemical-fluctuation statistics, local phase boundaries, and clustering indices mediate the macroscopic mechanical response.
The model should be enhanced by transfer learning from ab initio calculations.
The predictions apply at room temperature and controlled strain rates when the sample microstructure remains consistent with the training data.

Encoding microstructural heterogeneity in physically informed descriptors permits rapid extrapolation from simulations and experimental characterization without full-scale ab initio or CALPHAD calculations.
The workflow will improve prediction accuracy for Young’s modulus and yield strength by roughly 10%.
The workflow will reduce computational screening time by 30–50%.
The workflow will provide reasonable estimates of fracture toughness.
Ab initio calculations are too time-consuming for efficient high-throughput alloy screening.
CALPHAD screening can require significant computing resources.
Explicit prediction of alloy yield strength and fracture behavior is mostly beyond currently available DFT implementations.
Conventional machine-learning predictions are sensitive to the size and composition of their training datasets.
The model will become unreliable if unexpected secondary phases form or the characteristic chemical-fluctuation pattern is lost relative to the training set.
The model will become unreliable at extreme temperatures or loading rates outside its calibration regime.
Sample-preparation variability and difficulty encoding multiscale features make the exact accuracy and efficiency gains uncertain.
A blinded prospective benchmark should compare independent model predictions with modulus, tensile-yield, and standardized fracture measurements on hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 samples.
Prediction errors exceeding ±10% for Young’s modulus, ±15% for yield strength, or ±20% for fracture toughness constitute the proposed falsification criterion.
